list.listitem: Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning is one of the most common causes of accidental toxic poisonings and deaths. C
Suspect CO poisoning in patients with possible CO exposure and fatigue, dizziness, headache, unconsciousness, shortness of breath, and confusion.C
Initiate high flow normobaric 100% oxygen therapy immediately.C
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy improves CO elimination, and it may reduce the incidence and severity of neurologic sequelae, although clinical trial data are limited and somewhat inconsistent.B
Tissue hypoxia is due to the binding of CO to respiratory ligands such as hemoglobin (Hb) and myoglobin:
CO binds to hemoglobin with an affinity 230 to 270 times greater than oxygen.
This binding creates carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), which shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the left.
This results in increased ability of COHb to hold on to oxygen, reducing the availability of oxygen to metabolically active tissues.
Cellular poisoning is due to CO binding to the cytochrome P450 system:
This uncouples oxidative phosphorylation altering ATP production and causing intracellular acidosis.
Increased production of cardiac and skeletal myoglobin alters tissue oxygen uptake.
Myocardial depression due to hypoxic stress, cytochrome a3 dysfunction and binding to cardiac myoglobin resulting in cardiac ischemia.
Arterial hypotension leads to more myocardial depression and nitrous oxide related peripheral vasodilation.
Loss of consciousness occurs as a result of a reduction in cerebral perfusion and ischemic reperfusion injury can follow.
Neurovascular effects can be profound and long lasting:
CO in the circulation is associated with a massive increase in nitric oxide (NO) in perivascular tissues.
NO is also released from the vascular endothelial cells and platelets.
There is a production of oxygen radicals from impaired mitochondrial function.
A reaction between NO and oxygen radicals to form peroxynitrite which then binds to perivascular tissue proteins causing injury.
Patients commonly report headache, dizziness, loss of consciousness, altered mental status, weakness, muscle cramps, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, chest pain, dyspnea and memory loss. C
Order CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, urinalysis and arterial blood gas analyses with co-oximetry tests to include COHb levels. C
Obtain a chest radiograph and consider neuroimaging to exclude other diagnoses if clinically indicated. C

Obtain history and objective proof, if possible, of the inhaled poison and the duration of the exposure. Need to concentrate on neurologic complaints, cardiovascular complaints and other symptoms such as abdominal pain and muscle cramps.
Among the more common symptoms are headache, dizziness, loss of consciousness, altered mental status, weakness, muscle cramps, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, chest pain, dyspnea and memory loss.
Waterpipe-associated CO poisoning may be more likely to present with syncope than non-waterpipe-associated CO poisoning, according to a retrospective cohort study.
Check for housemates with similar symptoms.
Check for history of smoking and other possible exposures from automobiles or other sources of CO. Power outages may increase the risk of CO poisoning, particularly in children.
On physical exam, look for signs and symptoms of tissue hypoxia including neurologic deficits and cardiovascular abnormalities.
Some of the more common signs include ataxia, dysrhythmias, coma, skin blistering.
Fundoscopic findings like retinal hemorrhages and papilledema may be seen and suggest cerebral edema.

Order CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, urinalysis and arterial blood gas analyses with co-oximetry tests to include COHb levels. CO oximetry with spectrophotometry is the definitive test for diagnosis.
Pulse CO oximetry devices were found to be 77% sensitive and 83% specific, with an AUC of 0.86. The positive and negative likelihood ratios were 4.5 and 0.28 respectively.
COHb levels are elevated chronically in cigarette smokers; they also become less reliable the longer the delay from exposure, and do not always correlate with symptoms or outcomes.
In general, higher COHb levels correlate with poorer short-term outcomes, but do not correlate with more severe clinical features.
Heart-type fatty acid-binding protein may be useful as a biomarker for acute CO poisoning, with a cutoff of >1.5 ng/ml.
Order a chest x-ray in patients with cardiovascular or respiratory signs or symptoms. Consider neuroimaging for patients who are unconscious or have other neurologic symptoms.

A low serum netrin-1 level (<432 pg/ml) is an independent predictor of delayed neurologic sequelae and should be obtained if available (aOR 8.0, 95% CI 2.5-26). The sensitivity and specificity at that cutoff are 69% and 86%.
CK-MB and cardiac troponin can identify patients with acute cardiac damage due to CO poisoning.
Order an ECG to evaluate for arrhythmias or cardiac ischemia associated with hypoxemia.
Pregnancy test is mandatory of women of childbearing age as the unborn fetus is at greater risk than the mother because fetal Hb has a much higher affinity for CO than adult Hb.
Airway examination or direct laryngoscopy to assess inhalation injury in patients with burns.

Evaluate the patient for toxic coingestions in patients with non-accidental inhalation or suicide attempts. CO poisoning plus other toxic exposures is associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism and long-term mortality compared with CO poisoning alone.

For brain imaging in patients with symptoms of neurotoxicity. MRI is most useful in detecting early changes. Cerebral edema, globus pallidus hyperintensity, and white matter changes are most commonly seen.

section.type: Education about CO poisoning and the importance of CO monitoring is the key to prevention
section.heading: Education about CO poisoning and the importance of CO monitoring is the key to prevention

list.listitem: Install audible CO detectors as well as fire detectors in homes, offices, and the workplace.
Perform routine maintenance of home and office heating equipment, fireplaces, ovens as well as of all combustion engines.
Teach the signs and symptoms of CO poisoning and the need to seek medical attention for them.
Encourage people not to operate combustion appliances, engines, and vehicles within enclosed spaces.
Realize that the elderly, very young, and patients with chronic medical conditions such as heart disease are at increased risk.
Provide treatment and support for individuals with existing mental health disorders
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation). Intubate patients who are comatose or who are unable to protect their airway.
Utilize full ACLS measures as required for cardiac dysrhythmias.

A randomized trial in Turkey compared oxygen alone, metoclopramide plus oxygen, or metamizole plus oxygen for CO induced headache. There was no difference in outcomes at up to 4 hours for headache or nausea, and no patients required rescue medication.
All patients should have NBOT of 100% FiO2 via a high flow non-rebreathing mask as quickly as possible.
In patients with mild symptoms and COHb levels between 5% and 25% should have NBOT for at least 6 hours, and can be discharged when symptom free. or COHb level normalizes (3-5%)
Patients with moderate symptoms should be admitted overnight for continuous NBOT until symptom free.

Three to four months of daily 2-hour sessions breathing 100% oxygen from a tank or concentrator while supine via a nasal canulus at 6 to 10 liters per minute are usually sufficient to normalize PvO2 and obtain lasting relief from the most common symptoms of chronic CO poisoning.

HBO is the delivery of 100% oxygen at greater than atmospheric pressure, and this can shorten the half life of COHb dramatically. Some studies have shown that those effects help prevent CO-mediated brain injury.

Indications include altered mental status, coma or any abnormal neurologic exam, loss of consciousness, seizure, hypotension, myocardial depression, dysrhythmias, ischemia or infarction, or pregnancy with a COHb >15%.
Consider HBO for patients with elevated COHb levels >25%, regardless of symptoms.

A Cochrane review of HBO for CO poisoning suggests that existing HBO trials are inadequate to prove the benefit of HBO to reduce the incidence of adverse neurological events. They also suggest that more research, likely a large, multicenter randomized controlled trial would be necessary to define the role of HBO in CO poisoning.

A systematic review of 7 RCT with 2023 patients with CO poisoning were enrolled in this study. HBO was associated with a lower risk of memory impairment compared to patients receiving normobaric oxygen, and 2 sessions of HBO were associated with a higher risk of memory impairment compared to those who received 1 session of HBO. HBO was associated with improved neuropsychologic scores compared with NBO.

The American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) issued a clinical policy statement in 2007 discussing the critical issues in the management of adults with CO poisoning in the emergency department (ED). These recommendations are based on a thorough review of the medical literature relevant to the topic of HBO. As a Level C Recommendation, ACEP found that HBO may be a therapeutic option for CO poisoning, but its use cannot be mandated. They also found that no clinical variables, including COHb levels, identify a subgroup of CO poisoned patients for whom HBO is most likely to provide benefit or cause harm. Another review acknowledged the limitations of existing studies, but suggested that the most relevant study supported the benefits of HBO.

A systematic review identified 6 randomized trials of hyperbaric vs normobaric, with between 26 and 340 patients per study. They found modest benefits in terms of improved cognitive and neurologic symptoms, although the studies were at moderate risk of bias.
Side effects of HBO include seizure, oxygen toxicity and barotrauma to ears or lungs.

Sodium bicarbonate should be avoided, even in cases of significant metabolic acidosis. It forms CO2 when metabolized and this competes for a common elimination pathway as CO, which delays the clearance of both.
Hydroxocobalamin may be used if there is suspicion of concomitant cyanide poisoning (such as in house fires).Note that COHb levels may be spuriously elevated after administration.

A small study of 42 patients with delayed encephalopathy after CO poisoning found that the combination of mesenchymal stem cell transplantation and butylphthalide was more effective than HBO or stem cell transplant alone in terms of the Barthl index and Mini-Mental State examination.

A systematic review of Cochrane, Embase, Pubmed, and Web of Science databases identified 4 RCTs involving 435 patients with delayed encephalopathy after CO poisoning that evaluated the efficacy and treatment for these patients. It found that mesenchymal stem cell transplantation was superior to HBO. Also, adding dexamethasone, N-butylphthalide, or XingZhi-YiNao granules into HBO, or butylphthalide into mesenchymal stem cell transplantation achieved better neurological recovery in patients without a substantial increase in adverse events. Preliminary results are promising, but larger and longer studies are needed.

Independent predictors of delayed neurologic sequelae include low serum netrin-1 level (aOR: 8.0), low Glasgow coma scale on admission (aOR: 0.81), longer CO exposure time (AOR: 2.0), and the presence of acute brain lesions (aOR: 8.2).

A study assessing 60 patients with acute carbon monoxide poisoning investigated the association between levels of neuron-specific enolase (NSE) and S100B protein with coma duration. NSE and S100B protein were significantly correlated with the degree of impaired consciousness in individuals, and had the same clinical value in predicting coma duration ≥72 hours compared to GCS score. NSE levels >13 μg/L had a sensitivity and specificity of 80% and 64% respectively. S100B levels >0.43 μg/L had a sensitivity and specificity of 70% and 88% respectively. However, the sample size was small and a larger sample size is needed for further evaluation.

Risk factors for poor outcomes associated with CO poisoning include the following: age <6 years, age >65 years, cardiovascular and respiratory comorbidities, fetal exposure, prolonged exposure, and intentional exposure.
According to a Korean nationwide population-based cohort study of 48,600 patients, patients with a history of CO poisoning exhibit an increased all-cause mortality compared to matched controls.
